small_guidance:
- The matmul is huge (M=128, N=K=32768) and BLOCK_M=16/32 wastes tensor-core throughput since each row tile is tiny. Add configs with BLOCK_M=64 and BLOCK_M=128 (e.g. 128/128/32, 128/64/64, 64/128/64) with num_warps=8, num_stages=3-4 — M=128 means there are very few M tiles so larger BLOCK_M raises arithmetic intensity per program.
- Drop the two-pass partial buffer + reduce_partials_kernel: add a `tl.atomic_add` (or single-program-per-row split-K with atomic) into a length-M output, so the sigmoid-sum epilogue writes directly into `out[m]`. This removes a full M×n_tiles write/read round-trip.
- Add a GROUP_M=1 (or just remove grouping) swizzle since M is tiny relative to N; instead consider swapping grid so pid_n is the outer dim for better L2 reuse of the X rows across N tiles (X row of 32768 floats = 128KB, reused across all N tiles).
large_guidance:
- Restructure as split-K along N (the hidden dim being reduced after sigmoid): one program per (row, N-chunk), compute the GEMM tile, apply bias+sigmoid, reduce along N inside the program to a scalar, then `tl.atomic_add` into `out[m]`. This fuses everything into one kernel and eliminates the partial matrix entirely.
- Since K=32768 is the dot-product dim and N=32768 is reduced away, consider a persistent-per-row kernel: BLOCK_M=1 (or 4) rows resident, loop over N tiles of size BLOCK_N=256, each tile does a K-loop GEMV-style accumulation (since BLOCK_M is small this is effectively many GEMVs). With BLOCK_M=8 or 16 you can still use tl.dot. Key insight: each X row is read once and reused across all N — exploit this by keeping the row's K-chunks in registers/shared across the N loop, instead of re-reading X for every N tile.
- Alternative: cast weights/inputs to fp16/bf16 for the tl.dot (RTX 4090 has strong fp16 tensor cores, ~2x fp32), accumulating in fp32, since the final sigmoid+sum tolerates 5e-2.
